claim: Utah multi-electrode arrays were implanted in the arm representation of Brodmann's area 2 of S1 in three Rhesus macaques (Monkeys C, H, and L).
source: For the experiments detailed in this paper, we recorded neural signals from three Rhesus macaques (Monkeys C, H, and L) using Utah multi-electrode arrays (Blackrock Microsystems) implanted in the arm representation of Brodmann's area 2 of S1 (Figure 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the experimental setup.

claim: Both deep and cutaneous receptive fields were found across each array.
source: We found both deep and cutaneous receptive fields across each array, largely matching the description of area 2 from previous studies (Hyvärinen and Poranen, 1978; Pons et al., 1985; Seelke et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated observation from sensory mapping experiments, with supporting citations.

claim: Area 1 tends to have a higher fraction of cutaneous responses than area 2.
source: Of the two bordering regions, area 1 tends to have a higher fraction of cutaneous responses, and area 5 tends to have a higher fraction of deep responses (Seelke et al., 2012), suggesting that our arrays were implanted largely in area 2.
evidence: Cited from previous literature to support array placement.

claim: Area 5 tends to have a higher fraction of deep responses than area 2.
source: Of the two bordering regions, area 1 tends to have a higher fraction of cutaneous responses, and area 5 tends to have a higher fraction of deep responses (Seelke et al., 2012), suggesting that our arrays were implanted largely in area 2.
evidence: Cited from previous literature to support array placement.

claim: Monkeys C and H showed a rough proximal to distal arm gradient running from anterior to posterior across the array.
source: For Monkeys C and H, we found a rough proximal to distal arm gradient, running from anterior to posterior across the array (Figure 1, black arrows), consistent with the somatotopy found by Pons et al. (1985).
evidence: Directly stated observation from sensory mapping, shown in Figure 1, and compared to previous literature.

claim: The somatotopic gradient found in Monkeys C and H is consistent with the somatotopy found by Pons et al. (1985).
source: For Monkeys C and H, we found a rough proximal to distal arm gradient, running from anterior to posterior across the array (Figure 1, black arrows), consistent with the somatotopy found by Pons et al. (1985).
evidence: Comparison of current findings to previous literature.

claim: Monkey L had too few well-mapped neurons to determine a meaningful gradient.
source: There were too few well-mapped neurons from Monkey L to determine a meaningful gradient.
evidence: Directly stated limitation of the data from Monkey L.

claim: The whole-arm model out-performed the hand-only model in predicting neural activity.
source: We found that for this measure, the whole-arm model out-performed the hand-only model (Figure 4).
evidence: Directly stated result of model comparison, shown in Figure 4.

claim: 238 out of 288 neurons were significantly better predicted by the whole-arm model than the hand-only model.
source: Of the 288 neurons recorded across the 8 sessions, 238 were significantly better predicted by the whole-arm model than the hand-only model, and for the other 50, there was no significant difference (using p < 0.05; see Materials and methods for more details).
evidence: Directly stated statistical result from model comparison.

claim: For 50 out of 288 neurons, there was no significant difference between the whole-arm and hand-only models.
source: Of the 288 neurons recorded across the 8 sessions, 238 were significantly better predicted by the whole-arm model than the hand-only model, and for the other 50, there was no significant difference (using p < 0.05; see Materials and methods for more details).
evidence: Directly stated statistical result from model comparison.

claim: The whole-arm model explains neural variance as well as models trained in individual workspaces.
source: The symbols lying very close to the unity line in each panel of Figure 5 indicate that the full model explained just as much neural variance as did the individual models.
evidence: Directly stated result from comparing models trained on combined vs. individual workspaces, shown in Figure 5.

claim: The whole-arm model describes a consistent, generalizable relationship between neural activity and arm kinematics across the two workspaces.
source: This suggests that the whole-arm model describes a consistent, generalizable relationship between neural activity and arm kinematics across the two workspaces.
evidence: Inference drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: 260 out of 288 recorded neurons were significantly tuned to movement direction in both workspaces.
source: Of the 288 recorded neurons, 260 were significantly tuned to movement direction in both workspaces.
evidence: Directly stated statistical result from directional tuning analysis.

claim: The hand-only model predicted essentially the same tuning curve for both workspaces, with the exception of a baseline shift due to the position component.
source: As shown in the example in Figure 3D, the hand-only model predicted essentially the same tuning curve for both workspaces, with the exception of a baseline shift due to the position component.
evidence: Directly stated observation from the example neuron shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The whole-arm model predicted altered tuning curves that matched the actual ones well.
source: In contrast, the whole-arm model predicted altered tuning curves, which matched the actual ones well.
evidence: Directly stated observation from the example neuron analysis.

claim: Only two out of 288 neurons were significantly better predicted by the hand-only model in terms of tuning curve correlation.
source: Only two out of 288 neurons were significantly better predicted by the hand-only model (using p < 0.05), while 138 of 288 neurons were significantly better predicted by the whole-arm model.
evidence: Directly stated statistical result from tuning curve correlation analysis.

claim: 138 out of 288 neurons were significantly better predicted by the whole-arm model in terms of tuning curve correlation.
source: Only two out of 288 neurons were significantly better predicted by the hand-only model (using p < 0.05), while 138 of 288 neurons were significantly better predicted by the whole-arm model.
evidence: Directly stated statistical result from tuning curve correlation analysis.

claim: The whole-arm model had an average circular VAF of 0.75 for predicted PD changes.
source: Based on the circular VAF (cVAF; see Materials and methods for details) of the predicted PD changes, Figure 7B shows that the whole-arm model once again out-performed the hand-only model, with an average cVAF over all neurons of 0.75 compared to 0.57.
evidence: Directly stated statistical result from PD shift analysis, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The hand-only model had an average circular VAF of 0.57 for predicted PD changes.
source: Based on the circular VAF (cVAF; see Materials and methods for details) of the predicted PD changes, Figure 7B shows that the whole-arm model once again out-performed the hand-only model, with an average cVAF over all neurons of 0.75 compared to 0.57.
evidence: Directly stated statistical result from PD shift analysis, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In all but one session, the whole-arm model out-performed the hand-only model in predicting PD shifts.
source: We made pairwise comparisons between models for each session. In every session but one, the whole-arm model out-performed the hand-only model. In the remaining session, the difference between the two models was not significant (p > 0.05).
evidence: Directly stated statistical result from session-by-session model comparison.

claim: Whole-arm kinematics were highly separable between active and passive movements, with a linear discriminant analysis classifier predicting movement type 89% of the time on average.
source: Averaged over the sessions, a linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifier could predict the movement type 89% of the time, using only the whole-arm kinematics in the analysis window, meaning that these whole-arm kinematics were highly separable based on movement condition.
evidence: Directly stated result from LDA classification analysis.

claim: Many area 2 neurons had an above chance separability index for distinguishing active from passive movements.
source: We found that many neurons had an above chance separability index, as we would expect from neurons representing whole-arm kinematics.
evidence: Directly stated observation from separability analysis, shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Model consistency correlated negatively with the separability index.
source: Interestingly, we found the opposite result—model consistency actually correlated negatively with the separability index.
evidence: Directly stated result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 11.

claim: Neurons responding to active and passive movements differently are likely not drawing this distinction based on arm kinematics.
source: Essentially, this means that neurons responding to active and passive movements differently are likely not drawing this distinction based on arm kinematics, as those are the neurons for which we could not find a consistent whole-arm model.
evidence: Inference drawn from the negative correlation between model consistency and separability index.

claim: Neurons in area 2 may distinguish active and passive movements by means of an efference copy signal from motor areas of the brain.
source: Instead, this suggests that neurons in area 2 distinguish active and passive movements by some other means, perhaps an efference copy signal from motor areas of the brain (Bell, 1981; London and Miller, 2013; Nelson, 1987).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the results, with supporting citations.

claim: Area 2 of primary somatosensory cortex is likely important for mediating reach-related proprioception.
source: One brain area likely important for mediating reach-related proprioception is the proximal arm representation within area 2 of primary somatosensory cortex (S1) (Jennings et al., 1983; Kaas et al., 1979; London and Miller, 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Area 2 receives a combination of muscle and cutaneous inputs.
source: Though this area receives a combination of muscle and cutaneous inputs (Hyvärinen and Poranen, 1978; Padberg et al., 2019; Pons et al., 1985), the few studies examining it during reaching have found that a model involving simply the translation of the hand approximates neural activity quite well (London and Miller, 2013; London et al., 2011; Prud'homme and Kalaska, 1994; Weber et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies found that a model involving simply the translation of the hand approximates area 2 neural activity quite well during reaching.
source: Though this area receives a combination of muscle and cutaneous inputs (Hyvärinen and Poranen, 1978; Padberg et al., 2019; Pons et al., 1985), the few studies examining it during reaching have found that a model involving simply the translation of the hand approximates neural activity quite well (London and Miller, 2013; London et al., 2011; Prud'homme and Kalaska, 1994; Weber et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Humans are better at estimating the location of the hand than joint angles.
source: Interestingly, this finding fits with psychophysical data showing that humans are better at estimating the location of the hand than joint angles (Fuentes and Bastian, 2010), as well as our conscious experience of reaching to objects, which typically focuses on the hand.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to psychophysical study.

claim: Computational studies have shown that while neural activity may appear to be tuned to the state of a limb's endpoint, features of this tuning might be a direct consequence of the biomechanics of the limb.
source: However, recent computational studies have shown that while neural activity may appear to be tuned to the state of a limb's endpoint, features of this tuning might be a direct consequence of the biomechanics of the limb (Chowdhury et al., 2017; Lillicrap and Scott, 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to computational studies.

claim: Muscle lengths were better predictors of area 2 activity than were hand kinematics in artificial neural network models.
source: Consistent with those results, we have recently observed, using artificial neural networks, that muscle lengths were better predictors of area 2 activity than were hand kinematics (Lucas et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about previous findings from the same research group, supported by citation.

claim: Proprioception is critical for making coordinated movements.
source: Of the relevant sensory modalities, proprioception, or the sense of body position, movement and associated forces, is arguably the most critical for making coordinated movements (Ghez and Sainburg, 1995; Gordon et al., 1995; Sainburg et al., 1995; Sainburg et al., 1993; Sanes et al., 1984).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Few studies have explicitly addressed how proprioception is represented in the brain during natural movement.
source: However, despite its importance, few studies have explicitly addressed how proprioception is represented in the brain during natural movement; touch, vision, and the motor areas of the brain have received far more attention.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field, based on knowledge of the literature.

claim: Neural activity in area 2 includes representation of the whole arm during reaching.
source: These results suggest that 1) neural activity in area 2 includes representation of the whole arm during reaching and 2) many of these neurons represented limb state differently during active and passive movements.
evidence: Summary conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the experimental results.

claim: Many area 2 neurons represented limb state differently during active and passive movements.
source: These results suggest that 1) neural activity in area 2 includes representation of the whole arm during reaching and 2) many of these neurons represented limb state differently during active and passive movements.
evidence: Summary conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the experimental results.

claim: A whole-arm model successfully predicted how features of neural activity changed as monkeys reached to targets in two workspaces.
source: We found that a whole-arm model, unlike classic models, successfully predicted how features of neural activity changed as monkeys reached to targets in two workspaces.
evidence: Summary statement from the abstract about the main finding of the two-workspace experiment.

claim: Many neurons did not consistently represent the whole arm over both active and passive movement conditions.
source: However, when we then evaluated this whole-arm model across active and passive movements, we found that many neurons did not consistently represent the whole arm over both conditions.
evidence: Summary statement from the abstract about the main finding of the active/passive experiment.

claim: The hand-only model assumes neurons relate only to the Cartesian coordinates of hand position and velocity.
source: The hand-only model stems from classic, endpoint models of limb movement-related neural activity (Bosco et al., 2000; Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Prud'homme and Kalaska, 1994). It assumes neurons relate only to the Cartesian coordinates of hand position and velocity.
evidence: Direct description of the hand-only model used in the study.

claim: The whole-arm model builds on the hand-only model by adding the Cartesian kinematics (position and velocity) of the elbow.
source: The whole-arm model builds on the hand-only model by adding the Cartesian kinematics (position and velocity) of the elbow, in order to account more fully for movement of the whole arm.
evidence: Direct description of the whole-arm model used in the study.

claim: The performance of the whole-arm model was similar to, or even better than more complicated biomechanical models based on seven degree-of-freedom joint kinematics or musculotendon lengths.
source: Surprisingly, the performance of this representation of the whole arm was similar to, or even better than more complicated biomechanical models based on the seven degree-of-freedom joint kinematics or musculotendon lengths (see Appendix 1).
evidence: Statement about model comparison results detailed in Appendix 1.

claim: For the whole-arm model to be effective, it should explain the variance of neural firing rates across the two workspaces better than the hand-only model.
source: For us to consider the whole-arm model to be an effective one for area 2, it should satisfy three main criteria. First and most direct, it should explain the variance of neural firing rates across the two workspaces better than the hand-only model, as is the case in the example in Figure 3C.
evidence: Statement of evaluation criteria for the whole-arm model.

claim: For the whole-arm model to be effective, the mapping between neural activity and whole-arm kinematics should not change between the individual workspaces.
source: Second, the mapping between neural activity and whole-arm kinematics should not change between the individual workspaces, meaning that the accuracy of a model trained over both workspaces should be similar to that trained in a single workspace.
evidence: Statement of evaluation criteria for the whole-arm model.

claim: For the whole-arm model to be effective, it should be able to capture features of neural activity that it was not explicitly trained on, such as changes in directional tuning.
source: Last, the model should be able to capture features of neural activity that it was not explicitly trained on, for example, the changes in directional tuning shown in Figure 3D.
evidence: Statement of evaluation criteria for the whole-arm model.

claim: Random locations of targets lessened the stereotopy of movements, allowing for collection of more varied movement data than from a center-out paradigm.
source: This had two important effects. First, the random locations of the targets lessened the stereotopy of the movements, allowing for the collection of more varied movement data than from a center-out paradigm.
evidence: Explanation of the experimental design rationale.

claim: The average postures in the two workspaces were quite different.
source: Second, the average postures in the two workspaces were quite different, such that while the signals of different models were still correlated within a given workspace, this correlation (and the mapping between sets of behavioral signals) changed significantly between workspaces.
evidence: Statement about the behavioral differences between workspaces.

claim: The correlation between behavioral signals of different models changed significantly between workspaces.
source: Second, the average postures in the two workspaces were quite different, such that while the signals of different models were still correlated within a given workspace, this correlation (and the mapping between sets of behavioral signals) changed significantly between workspaces.
evidence: Statement about how the experimental design affects model predictions.

claim: The different correlations between workspaces forced the models to make different predictions of neural activity across the two workspaces.
source: This forced the models to make different predictions of neural activity across the two workspaces.
evidence: Explanation of how the experimental design enables model discrimination.

claim: By comparing modeled and observed changes in neural activity, the study could more reliably discriminate between models.
source: By comparing modeled and observed changes in neural activity, we could more reliably discriminate between models.
evidence: Explanation of the analytical approach.

claim: Three two-workspace sessions were recorded with each of Monkeys C and H.
source: We recorded three of these two-workspace sessions with each of Monkeys C and H and two sessions with Monkey L.
evidence: Direct statement about the number of recording sessions.

claim: Two two-workspace sessions were recorded with Monkey L.
source: We recorded three of these two-workspace sessions with each of Monkeys C and H and two sessions with Monkey L.
evidence: Direct statement about the number of recording sessions.

claim: The active/passive experiment included two sessions with each of Monkeys C and H.
source: This experiment included two sessions with each of Monkeys C and H.
evidence: Direct statement about the number of recording sessions.

claim: Behavior and neural activity were analyzed only during the 120 ms after movement onset for which the kinematics of the hand were similar in active and passive trials.
source: As in the earlier study performed by our group (London and Miller, 2013), we analyzed behavior and neural activity only during the 120 ms after movement onset for which the kinematics of the hand were similar in active and passive trials (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: Direct statement about the analysis window, with reference to previous study and figures.

claim: The 120 ms analysis window is the time period in which there is not expected to be a voluntary reaction to the bumps in the passive trials.
source: This is also the time period in which we can reasonably expect there not to be a voluntary reaction to the bumps in the passive trials.
evidence: Explanation of the rationale for the analysis window choice.

claim: Average movement speed was similar between active and passive trials in the 120 ms analysis window.
source: However, average movement speed was similar between active and passive trials in this 120 ms window, which we used for data analysis.
evidence: Statement about behavioral similarity in the analysis window, shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Starting around 120 ms after movement onset, a bimodal distribution in passive movement speed emerges.
source: Starting around 120 ms after movement onset, a bimodal distribution in passive movement speed emerges.
evidence: Observation from Figure 8B about the time course of passive movements.

claim: The bimodality in passive movement speed reflects differences in the impedance of the arm for different directions of movement.
source: This bimodality reflects differences in the impedance of the arm for different directions of movement.
evidence: Interpretation of the bimodal distribution in passive movement speed.

claim: Perturbations towards and away from the body tended to result in a shorter overall movement than those to the left or right.
source: Perturbations towards and away from the body tended to result in a shorter overall movement than those to the left or right.
evidence: Observation about directional differences in passive movements.

claim: Area 2 neurons had a wide range of sensitivities to active and passive hand movements.
source: As reported earlier, area 2 neurons had a wide range of sensitivities to active and passive hand movements (London and Miller, 2013).
evidence: Statement about neural responses, with citation to previous study.

claim: Voluntary movements may change the afferent activity from the moving limb due to altered descending gamma drive to muscle spindles.
source: This could be caused by altered descending gamma drive to muscle spindles that changes their sensitivity (Loeb et al., 1985; Prochazka and Wand, 1981; Prochazka et al., 1976).
evidence: Speculative explanation for differences between active and passive movements, with supporting citations.

claim: An efference copy signal may be sent to the brainstem or S1 from motor areas during active movements.
source: Another possibility is that of an efference copy signal sent to the brainstem or S1 from motor areas during active movements (Bell, 1981; London and Miller, 2013; Nelson, 1987).
evidence: Speculative explanation for differences between active and passive movements, with supporting citations.

claim: Many studies suggest that we use internal forward models of our bodies and the environment to coordinate our movements and predict their sensory consequences.
source: Many studies suggest that we use internal forward models of our bodies and the environment to coordinate our movements and predict their sensory consequences (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994; Wolpert et al., 1995).
evidence: Statement about theoretical framework, supported by citations.

claim: A key piece of the internal forward model framework is comparing the actual feedback received following movement with the feedback predicted by the internal model, which generates a sensory prediction error.
source: A key piece of this framework is comparing the actual feedback received following movement with the feedback predicted by the internal model, which generates a sensory prediction error.
evidence: Explanation of theoretical framework.

claim: Recent studies suggest that S1 is important for updating the internal model using a sensory prediction error.
source: Recent studies suggest that S1 is important for updating the internal model using a sensory prediction error (Mathis et al., 2017; Nasir et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about S1 function, supported by citations.

claim: One potential avenue to study the effect of efference copy in S1 would be to examine how motor areas communicate with area 2 during active and passive movements.
source: Thus, one potential avenue to study the effect of efference copy in S1 would be to examine how motor areas communicate with area 2 during active and passive movements.
evidence: Suggestion for future research direction.

claim: As BCI for motor control gets more advanced, it will become more necessary to develop a method to provide feedback about movements to the brain.
source: As BCI for motor control gets more advanced (Collinger et al., 2013; Ethier et al., 2012; Kao et al., 2015; Young et al., 2019), it will become more necessary to develop a method to provide feedback about movements to the brain, potentially using intracortical microstimulation (ICMS) to activate somatosensory areas.
evidence: Statement about future BCI needs, with supporting citations.

claim: The use of ICMS in S1 has led to some success in providing feedback about touch.
source: While the use of ICMS in S1 has led to some success in providing feedback about touch (Flesher et al., 2016; Romo et al., 1998; Armenta Salas et al., 2018; Tabot et al., 2013), the path towards providing proprioceptive feedback remains relatively unexplored.
evidence: Statement about current state of ICMS research, with supporting citations.

claim: The path towards providing proprioceptive feedback using ICMS remains relatively unexplored.
source: While the use of ICMS in S1 has led to some success in providing feedback about touch (Flesher et al., 2016; Romo et al., 1998; Armenta Salas et al., 2018; Tabot et al., 2013), the path towards providing proprioceptive feedback remains relatively unexplored.
evidence: Statement about gap in current research.

claim: At least one study used electrical stimulation in S1 for feedback during movement, using the stimulation to specify target direction with respect to the evolving hand position.
source: At least one study did use electrical stimulation in S1 for feedback during movement, using the stimulation to specify target direction with respect to the evolving hand position (Dadarlat et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about previous ICMS study, with citation.

claim: The target-error information provided by ICMS in the Dadarlat et al. study is very different from the information normally encoded by S1.
source: However, this target-error information is very different from the information normally encoded by S1, and the monkeys required several months to learn to use it.
evidence: Interpretation of the Dadarlat et al. study results.

claim: Monkeys in the Dadarlat et al. study required several months to learn to use the ICMS feedback.
source: However, this target-error information is very different from the information normally encoded by S1, and the monkeys required several months to learn to use it.
evidence: Statement about the Dadarlat et al. study results.

claim: No study has yet shown a way to use ICMS to provide biomimetic proprioceptive feedback during reaching.
source: To our knowledge, no study has yet shown a way to use ICMS to provide more biomimetic proprioceptive feedback during reaching.
evidence: Statement about gap in current research.

claim: In one monkey, ICMS delivered simultaneously with a mechanical bump to the arm biased the monkey's perception of the bump direction toward the electrodes' PD.
source: In one monkey, ICMS delivered simultaneously with a mechanical bump to the arm biased the monkey's perception of the bump direction toward the electrodes' PD (Tomlinson and Miller, 2016).
evidence: Statement about previous study results from the same lab, with citation.

claim: The ICMS result from Tomlinson and Miller (2016) could not be replicated in other monkeys.
source: Unfortunately, the result could not be replicated in other monkeys; while the ICMS often biased their reports, the direction of the bias could not be explained by the PDs of the stimulated electrodes.
evidence: Statement about replication failure in previous study.

claim: One potential reason for the ICMS replication failure may be that the stimulation paradigm was derived from the classic, hand-based model and the assumption that area 2 represents active and passive movements similarly.
source: One potential reason may be that the stimulation paradigm in those experiments was derived from the classic, hand-based model and the assumption that area 2 represents active and passive movements similarly.
evidence: Speculative explanation for previous study's replication failure, based on current findings.

claim: It is possible that a stimulation paradigm based on a whole-arm model may be more successful for ICMS.
source: It is possible that a stimulation paradigm based on a whole-arm model may be more successful.
evidence: Speculative suggestion for future ICMS research based on current findings.

claim: Sensation for perception versus action is thought to arise from processing in two distinct pathways.
source: Another important consideration is the difference between sensation for perception versus action, which which is thought to arise from processing in two distinct pathways (Dijkerman and de Haan, 2007; Mishkin and Ungerleider, 1982; Sedda and Scarpina, 2012).
evidence: Statement about theoretical framework, with supporting citations.

claim: Most studies using ICMS have tended to engage the perceptual rather than the action stream of proprioception.
source: Most studies using ICMS have tended to engage the perceptual rather than the action stream of proprioception, either by using perceptual reporting of the effects of ICMS (Armenta Salas et al., 2018; Tomlinson and Miller, 2016; Zaaimi et al., 2013), or by using ICMS as a conscious sensory substitute for prorioceptive feedback (Dadarlat et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about current ICMS research approaches, with supporting citations.

claim: The goal is to forge a way towards a stimulation paradigm in which both perceptual and action streams can be engaged, to enable users of a BCI both to perceive their limb and to respond rapidly to movement perturbations.
source: However, as we better characterize how S1 represents movements, we hope to forge a way towards a stimulation paradigm in which we can engage both streams, to enable users of a BCI both to perceive their limb, and to respond rapidly to movement perturbations.
evidence: Statement of future research goal.

claim: Signals predicted by the various whole-arm models have a one-to-one (albeit nonlinear) relationship to each other.
source: In contrast, signals predicted by the various whole-arm models (see Appendix 1) do have a one-to-one (albeit nonlinear) relationship to each other.
evidence: Statement about the mathematical relationship between different whole-arm model representations.

claim: Knowledge of the hand and elbow position should completely determine estimated joint angles and musculotendon lengths.
source: Knowledge of the hand and elbow position should completely determine estimated joint angles and musculotendon lengths, indicating that these models should have the same informational content.
evidence: Statement about the mathematical relationship between kinematic representations.

claim: A comparison between whole-arm models with one-to-one correspondence is purely one of coordinate frame.
source: As such, a comparison between these models (as in the Appendix 1) is purely one of coordinate frame.
evidence: Interpretation of what the comparison between whole-arm models tests.

claim: Comparisons between coordinate frames only make sense when using linear models to relate neural activity to behavior.
source: One major issue is that these comparisons only make sense when using linear models to relate neural activity to behavior.
evidence: Statement about limitations of coordinate frame comparisons.

claim: Once nonlinear models are considered, coordinate frames with one-to-one correspondence become nearly equivalent and much more difficult to compare meaningfully.
source: Once nonlinear models are considered, as in our study with artificial neural networks (Lucas et al., 2019), coordinate frames with one-to-one correspondence become nearly equivalent, and much more difficult to compare meaningfully.
evidence: Statement about limitations of coordinate frame comparisons with nonlinear models, with citation to related work.

claim: Over the last few decades, a controversy involving the exact nature of the neural representation of movement has played itself out in the literature surrounding motor cortex.
source: Over the last few decades, a controversy involving the exact nature of the neural representation of movement has played itself out in the literature surrounding motor cortex, with some advocating a hand-based representation of motor control (Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Georgopoulos et al., 1986; Moran and Schwartz, 1999) and others a muscle-based representation (Evarts, 1968; Fetz et al., 1989; Morrow et al., 2007; Oby et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about historical debate in motor control field, with supporting citations.

claim: The motor control field recently started turning away from questions of coordinate frame and towards questions of neural population dynamics and information processing.
source: Recently, the motor control field started turning away from questions of coordinate frame and towards questions of neural population dynamics and information processing (Churchland et al., 2010; Elsayed et al., 2016; Gallego et al., 2017; Kaufman et al., 2014; Perich et al., 2018; Russo et al., 2018; Sussillo et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about recent trends in motor control research, with supporting citations.

claim: Part of the motivation for the pivot away from coordinate frame questions is that it became increasingly clear that a 'pure' coordinate frame of movement representation is unlikely to exist.
source: Part of the motivation for this pivot in viewpoint is that it became increasingly clear that a 'pure' coordinate frame of movement representation is unlikely to exist (Fetz, 1992; Kakei et al., 1999).
evidence: Statement about reasons for shift in research focus, with supporting citations.

claim: Studies tended to use correlation between neural activity and behavioral variables as evidence that the neurons represent movements in a particular coordinate frame.
source: Further, studies tended to use correlation between neural activity and behavioral variables as evidence that the neurons represent movements in a particular coordinate frame.
evidence: Statement about common approach in previous research.

claim: Correlations between neural activity and behavioral variables could often be explained by multiple coordinate frames, casting doubt on the conclusiveness of the exact coordinate frame of representation.
source: However, as noted above, these correlations could often be explained by multiple coordinate frames, casting doubt on the conclusiveness of the exact coordinate frame of representation (Mussa-Ivaldi, 1988).
evidence: Statement about limitations of correlation-based approaches, with supporting citation.

claim: The study put aside the question of the coordinate frame of area 2, focusing instead on what can be gained by modeling area 2 in terms of whole-arm kinematics.
source: Consequently, in our study, we put aside the question of the coordinate frame of area 2, focusing instead on what we can gain by modeling area 2 in terms of whole-arm kinematics.
evidence: Statement about the study's approach and focus.

claim: A major question this study leaves open is that of how information about reaching is processed by different areas of the proprioceptive neuraxis.
source: A major question this study leaves open is that of how information about reaching is processed by different areas of the proprioceptive neuraxis.
evidence: Statement about limitations and future directions.

claim: A muscle spindle-like representation might be expected at the level of the dorsal root ganglia or the cuneate nucleus.
source: While we might expect a muscle spindle-like representation at the level of the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) or the cuneate nucleus, downstream from the receptors by only one and two synapses, respectively, this representation likely changes as the signals propagate through thalamus and into S1.
evidence: Speculative statement about expected representations at different levels of the proprioceptive pathway.

claim: The representation of proprioceptive information likely changes as signals propagate through thalamus and into S1.
source: While we might expect a muscle spindle-like representation at the level of the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) or the cuneate nucleus, downstream from the receptors by only one and two synapses, respectively, this representation likely changes as the signals propagate through thalamus and into S1.
evidence: Speculative statement about transformation of proprioceptive information.

claim: Different areas of S1 may have different representations of proprioceptive information.
source: Different areas of S1 may also have different representations.
evidence: Speculative statement about heterogeneity within S1.

claim: Area 3a receives input mostly from muscle afferents.
source: Area 3a, which receives input mostly from muscle afferents (Heath et al., 1976; Kaas et al., 1979; Phillips et al., 1971; Yamada et al., 2016), seems more likely to retain a muscle-like representation than is area 2, which integrates muscle afferent input with that from cutaneous receptors (Hyvärinen and Poranen, 1978; Padberg et al., 2019; Pons et al., 1985).
evidence: Statement about area 3a inputs, with supporting citations.

claim: Area 3a seems more likely to retain a muscle-like representation than area 2.
source: Area 3a, which receives input mostly from muscle afferents (Heath et al., 1976; Kaas et al., 1979; Phillips et al., 1971; Yamada et al., 2016), seems more likely to retain a muscle-like representation than is area 2, which integrates muscle afferent input with that from cutaneous receptors (Hyvärinen and Poranen, 1978; Padberg et al., 2019; Pons et al., 1985).
evidence: Speculative comparison between area 3a and area 2, based on their inputs.

claim: Area 2 integrates muscle afferent input with that from cutaneous receptors.
source: Area 3a, which receives input mostly from muscle afferents (Heath et al., 1976; Kaas et al., 1979; Phillips et al., 1971; Yamada et al., 2016), seems more likely to retain a muscle-like representation than is area 2, which integrates muscle afferent input with that from cutaneous receptors (Hyvärinen and Poranen, 1978; Padberg et al., 2019; Pons et al., 1985).
evidence: Statement about area 2 inputs, with supporting citations.

claim: Area 5 may have an even higher-level representation than area 2.
source: Likewise, area 5 may have an even higher-level representation, as it receives input from both somatosensory (Mountcastle et al., 1975) and motor cortices (Padberg et al., 2019), and appears to depend on attention (Chapman et al., 1984; Omrani et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculative statement about area 5 representation, based on its inputs and properties cited from literature.

claim: Area 5 receives input from both somatosensory and motor cortices.
source: Likewise, area 5 may have an even higher-level representation, as it receives input from both somatosensory (Mountcastle et al., 1975) and motor cortices (Padberg et al., 2019), and appears to depend on attention (Chapman et al., 1984; Omrani et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about area 5 inputs, with supporting citations.

claim: Area 5 appears to depend on attention.
source: Likewise, area 5 may have an even higher-level representation, as it receives input from both somatosensory (Mountcastle et al., 1975) and motor cortices (Padberg et al., 2019), and appears to depend on attention (Chapman et al., 1984; Omrani et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about area 5 properties, with supporting citations.

claim: It is becoming increasingly feasible to record from several proprioceptive areas simultaneously.
source: As it becomes increasingly feasible to record from several of these areas simultaneously (Richardson et al., 2016; Suresh et al., 2017; Weber et al., 2006), future experiments could examine how these areas project information to each other, as has been explored in motor and premotor cortices (Churchland et al., 2010; Elsayed et al., 2016; Kaufman et al., 2014; Perich et al., 2018), without modeling the more complex cortical areas explicitly in terms of particular behavioral variables 'encoded' by single neurons.
evidence: Statement about technological advances, with supporting citations.

claim: Future experiments could examine how proprioceptive areas project information to each other, as has been explored in motor and premotor cortices.
source: As it becomes increasingly feasible to record from several of these areas simultaneously (Richardson et al., 2016; Suresh et al., 2017; Weber et al., 2006), future experiments could examine how these areas project information to each other, as has been explored in motor and premotor cortices (Churchland et al., 2010; Elsayed et al., 2016; Kaufman et al., 2014; Perich et al., 2018), without modeling the more complex cortical areas explicitly in terms of particular behavioral variables 'encoded' by single neurons.
evidence: Suggestion for future research direction, with citations to analogous work in motor cortex.

claim: Goodness-of-fit metrics like R2 or variance-accounted-for (VAF) are ill-suited to the Poisson-like statistics of neural activity.
source: Goodness-of-fit metrics like R2 or variance-accounted-for (VAF) are ill-suited to the Poisson-like statistics of neural activity; instead, we used the likelihood-based pseudo-R2 (Cameron and Windmeijer, 1997; Cameron and Windmeijer, 1996; McFadden, 1977).
evidence: Statement about methodological choice, with supporting citations.

claim: Pseudo-R2 has a maximum value of 1 but can be negative for models that fail even to predict the mean firing rate during cross-validation.
source: Like VAF, pseudo-R2 has a maximum value of 1, but it can be negative for models that fail even to predict the mean firing rate during cross-validation.
evidence: Description of the pseudo-R2 metric properties.

claim: The values corresponding to a good fit are lower for pR2 than for either R2 or VAF, with a value of 0.2 usually considered a 'good' fit.
source: In general, the values corresponding to a good fit are lower for pR2 than for either R2 or VAF, with a value of 0.2 usually considered a 'good' fit (McFadden, 1977).
evidence: Statement about interpretation of pseudo-R2 values, with supporting citation.

claim: It is possible that neurons with inconsistent linear relationships to arm kinematics may simply reflect a single nonlinear relationship, requiring different linear approximations in the two zones.
source: Following the analogy of fitting a line to data distributed on an exponential curve, it is possible that the neurons with inconsistent linear relationships to arm kinematics may simply reflect a single nonlinear relationship, requiring different linear approximations in the two zones.
evidence: Speculative alternative explanation for inconsistent model fits.

claim: Several neurons with inconsistent relationships across conditions had high pR2 for models trained within condition.
source: Indeed, several of these neurons had high pR2 for models trained within condition (top left quadrants of Figure 10).
evidence: Observation supporting the nonlinearity hypothesis, shown in Figure 10.

claim: All surgical and experimental procedures were approved by the institutional animal care and use committee of Northwestern University under protocol #IS00000367.
source: All surgical and experimental procedures were fully consistent with the guide for the care and use of laboratory animals and approved by the institutional animal care and use committee of Northwestern University under protocol #IS00000367.
evidence: Statement about ethical approval.

claim: The monkeys received a pulse of juice or water as a reward after each successful reaching trial.
source: After each successful reaching trial, the monkey received a pulse of juice or water as a reward.
evidence: Description of behavioral training procedure.

claim: The position of the manipulandum handle was recorded using encoders on the manipulandum joints.
source: We recorded the position of the handle using encoders on the manipulandum joints.
evidence: Description of data collection method.

claim: The interaction forces between the monkey's hand and the handle were recorded using a six-axis load cell mounted underneath the handle.
source: We also recorded the interaction forces between the monkey's hand and the handle using a six-axis load cell mounted underneath the handle.
evidence: Description of data collection method.

claim: For the two-workspace experiment, the full workspace was partitioned into four 10 cm x 10 cm quadrants.
source: For the two-workspace experiment, we partitioned the full workspace into four 10 cm x 10 cm quadrants.
evidence: Description of experimental design.

claim: The far ipsilateral quadrant and the near contralateral quadrant were chosen for comparing neural representations of movement.
source: Of these four quadrants, we chose the far ipsilateral one and the near contralateral one in which to compare neural representations of movement.
evidence: Description of experimental design.

claim: Before each trial in the two-workspace experiment, one of the two workspaces was chosen randomly.
source: Before each trial, we chose one of the two workspaces randomly, within which the monkey reached to a short sequence of targets randomly positioned in the workspace.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.

claim: For the two-workspace experiment, only the portion of data from the end of the center-hold period to the end of the trial was analyzed.
source: For this experiment, we only analyzed the portion of data from the end of the center-hold period to the end of the trial.
evidence: Description of data analysis approach.

claim: In the active vs. passive experiment, the monkey performed a classic center-out reaching task.
source: For the active vs. passive experiment, we had the monkey perform a classic center-out (CO) reaching task, as described in London and Miller (2013).
evidence: Description of experimental task, with citation to previous study.

claim: On 50% of the trials in the active vs. passive experiment, a 2 N perturbation was delivered to the monkey's hand during the center hold period.
source: On 50% of the trials (deemed 'passive' trials), during the center hold period, we used motors on the manipulandum to deliver a 2 N perturbation to the monkey's hand in one of the four target directions.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.

claim: Ten markers of four different colors were painted on the outside of the monkey's arm before each reaching experiment.
source: Before each reaching experiment, we painted 10 markers of four different colors on the outside of the monkey's arm, marking bony landmarks and a few points in between, a la (Chan and Moran, 2006).
evidence: Description of motion tracking setup, with citation.

claim: A custom motion tracking system built from a Microsoft Kinect was used to record the 3D locations of markers.
source: Using a custom motion tracking system built from a Microsoft Kinect, we recorded the 3D locations of these markers with respect to the camera, synced in time to the other behavioral and neural data.
evidence: Description of motion tracking system.

claim: The Kinect-measured marker locations were aligned to the spatial lab frame by aligning location of the Kinect hand marker to the location of the handle in the manipulandum coordinate frame.
source: We then aligned the Kinect-measured marker locations to the spatial lab frame by aligning location of the Kinect hand marker to the location of the handle in the manipulandum coordinate frame.
evidence: Description of data processing method.

claim: The Cerebus recording system sampled signals from each of the 96 electrodes at 30 kHz.
source: This recording system sampled signals from each of the 96 electrodes at 30 kHz.
evidence: Description of neural recording parameters.

claim: The Cerebus system detected spikes online using a threshold set at −5x signal RMS.
source: To conserve data storage space, the system detected spikes online using a threshold set at −5x signal RMS, and only wrote to disk a time stamp and the 1.6 ms snippet of signal surrounding the threshold crossing.
evidence: Description of spike detection method.

claim: Plexon Offline Sorter was used to manually sort spike snippets into putative single units.
source: After data collection, we used Plexon Offline Sorter to manually sort these snippets into putative single units, using features like waveform shape and inter-spike interval.
evidence: Description of spike sorting method.

claim: For the two-workspace analyses, both behavioral variables and neural firing rate were averaged over 50 ms bins.
source: For the two-workspace analyses, both behavioral variables and neural firing rate were averaged over 50 ms bins.
evidence: Description of data processing method.

claim: For the active/passive analyses, behavioral variables and neural firing rates were averaged over the 120 ms period following movement onset in each trial.
source: For the active/passive analyses, we averaged behavioral variables and neural firing rates over the 120 ms period following movement onset in each trial.
evidence: Description of data processing method.

claim: Neural activity was modeled with respect to behavior using Poisson generalized linear models.
source: We modeled neural activity with respect to the behavior using Poisson generalized linear models (outline in Truccolo et al., 2005) shown in Equation 2a, below.
evidence: Description of modeling approach, with citation.

claim: Repeated 5-fold cross-validation was used to evaluate models of neural activity.
source: We used repeated 5-fold cross-validation to evaluate our models of neural activity, given that the models had different numbers of parameters, P.
evidence: Description of model evaluation method.

claim: The cross-validation process was repeated 20 times, resulting in n=100 sample size for each analysis result.
source: This process (including random splitting) was repeated 20 times, resulting in n=100 sample size for each analysis result.
evidence: Description of statistical analysis approach.

claim: A corrected resampled t-test was used to perform statistical tests on the output of repeated 5-fold cross-validation.
source: To perform statistical tests on the output of repeated 5-fold cross-validation, we used a corrected resampled t-test, outlined in Ernst (2017) and Nadeau and Bengio (2003).
evidence: Description of statistical testing method, with citations.

claim: All statistical tests were performed within individual sessions or for individual neurons, never across sessions or monkeys.
source: Note that we performed all statistical tests within individual sessions or for individual neurons, never across sessions or monkeys.
evidence: Description of statistical analysis approach.

claim: A Bonferroni correction factor of 6 was used for pairwise model comparisons.
source: Despite only making one pairwise comparison in the main text, we chose to use a Bonferroni correction factor of 6: three for the original three pairwise comparisons and one more for each additional model we tested, which were compared against the best model at the time, and could have changed the end result of this project.
evidence: Description of statistical correction approach.
